card.hook: Some days the Golden Gate Bridge simply isn't there, because fog has swallowed it whole. On a clear day, though, this is the postcard view everyone has seen, and you get to stand right in it.
card.stand_here: Head to Battery Spencer on the Marin Headlands side, reached from Conzelman Road, and face south. The bridge lies south of you, seen nearly side-on from above, with the north tower close and San Francisco and the bay behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower, the span and the city into one frame. Then try 1x for a cleaner, more natural look. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the north tower or pull the city closer to the bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky and the orange paint keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise, early morning or sunset, when soft light or drifting fog makes the bridge stand out. Fog can hide the bridge completely, so check conditions before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Use Battery Spencer, the overlook on the bluffs above the bridge. Turn on your front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and stand with the full length of the bridge over your shoulder and the San Francisco skyline in the same frame. If the Kirby Cove rope swing is up (about a mile down a gravel road, and it's not always there), a swinging selfie puts the bridge right behind you.
card.ask_someone: At Baker Beach, walk west along the beach so the whole bridge fits in the frame (the eastern end cuts part of it off), then hand your phone to a passer-by and pose with the bridge behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay behind any barriers and keep clear of the road. Drones are prohibited, and if you're on the bridge itself, watch for cyclists and take care with selfie sticks because the sidewalk is narrow. One source says the northern part of Baker Beach is clothing-optional.
card.challenge: Line the north tower up with a gridline, let the span run diagonally, and squeeze the city into the gap behind it. Bonus points if you keep a bit of headland in the corner.
card.good_to_know: The Golden Gate Bridge opened on 27 May 1937, when it was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world. The main span is 1,280 m and the total height is 227 m. A travel guide has called it the most photographed bridge in the world, and the view from Battery Spencer is free.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Battery Spencer on the Marin Headlands side, reached from Conzelman Road, and face south. The bridge lies south of you, seen nearly side-on from above, with the north tower close and San Francisco and the bay behind it.

card.hook: Alcatraz looks like a flat-topped pebble floating on the bay, and at normal zoom it's a lot smaller than you'd expect. Have a quick look at the bay before you walk all the way out, because fog can hide it completely.
card.stand_here: Head to Pier 39 and walk to the far (back) side, past the sea lions. Face north-west and Alcatraz sits centred across the open water.
card.zoom: Zoom 2x, or a touch more if your phone lets you, so the island fills a good part of the frame. At 1x it's lost in a big empty bay, and at 0.5x it's even smaller.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the island on the centre or lower-third line with lots of sky above, then tap the island and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Golden hour or early morning gives the warmest light, while summer midday can look harsh. Fog can hide the island at any time, so if it's gone, come back and try again.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the far end of Pier 39, past the sea lion area, facing the open bay, which gives the clearest backdrop of Alcatraz. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if it has it) and hold it a bit low so the island sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the far side of Pier 39, at the end nearest the bay, with you standing in front of the island so the whole rock is in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks and monopods aren't allowed inside the cellhouse or on the ferry. Gusts on the island can be strong, so keep a firm grip on your phone. Visiting the island itself needs a ferry and may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you keep the horizon dead level and get the whole island on a gridline, with you grinning in the corner of the shot?
card.good_to_know: Alcatraz began as a lighthouse site and a military fort, and from 1934 it was a federal prison until it closed on 21 March 1963. Today it's run by the National Park Service as a National Historic Landmark. It still has the oldest operating lighthouse on the West Coast, and nearly 1.4 million people visit each year.

card.hook: Here's a Wharf secret: the best photo isn't one famous landmark. It's the mix of old ships, open bay and waterfront buildings all in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand at the entrance to Hyde Street Pier and look southwest. You'll see Ghirardelli Square and the waterfront, with the old ships moored close by. The busy main Wharf is behind you to the east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the sweep towards Ghirardelli Square. Switch to 0.5x to squeeze in the masts and rigging. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the Golden Gate Bridge across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the waterfront along the top third, keep a ship's hull or rigging in the foreground, and tap the ships so they look sharp, then make the shot a touch darker if the sky and water look washed out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the waterfront. Early morning is typically quieter if you want the ships without people in them.
card.selfie_here: Head to the round wooden Fisherman's Wharf sign at the corner of Jefferson and Taylor Streets. Use the front camera, stand in front of the sign so it's behind you, and try 0.5x if you want more of it in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Hyde Street Pier is part of a national park site and has been reported closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go. Pier 39 has been reported closed too, so check its status as well. If the pier entrance is closed, the lettered Fisherman's Wharf sign or Aquatic Park both make good alternatives.
card.challenge: Get a ship's rigging in the foreground with Ghirardelli Square behind it, then spin around and catch the Golden Gate Bridge for shot number two.
card.good_to_know: Fisherman's Wharf began as a working fishing port, and in 1900 the state set this shoreline aside for commercial fishing boats. The docks declined in the 1960s and 1970s as tourism took over, but a few old family-run seafood restaurants are still here. Aquatic Park has a sheltered cove, a curved pier and a Streamline Moderne bathhouse, with the bay beyond.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the entrance to Hyde Street Pier and look southwest. You'll see Ghirardelli Square and the waterfront, with the old ships moored close by. The busy main Wharf is behind you to the east.

card.hook: Eight hairpin bends, red bricks and a car creeping down them like it's trying not to wake the neighbours: that's the block everyone pictures when they hear Lombard Street. Here's where to stand to get it all in one shot.
card.stand_here: Head to the corner of Leavenworth Street and Lombard Street, at the bottom (east) end of the crooked block, and stay on the sidewalk. Face uphill and the whole stack of curves, flower beds and houses rises up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole run of bends in one frame. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to home in on the curves and flower beds. Want more houses and sky? Try 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the street, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out the red bricks and flowers.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet for a clear view before the crowds arrive. The street sees around two million visitors a year (as of 2015), so it gets busy.
card.selfie_here: Try the pedestrian stairs halfway down the block, beside the flower beds. Use the front camera and keep the zigzag road behind you, with the flowers close in your frame. For a different backdrop, stand at the top corner of Hyde Street and Lombard Street, with the street dropping away behind you and the view east toward Coit Tower and the bay.
card.ask_someone: At the Leavenworth and Lombard corner, on the public sidewalk, hand your phone to a passer-by and pose with the switchbacks climbing up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so keep to the sidewalk, stay out of the flower beds and don't block driveways. At the top, stay off the road and the cable car tracks, because cable cars don't stop for people standing on them.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the people and cars, then try to catch a clear bend with not a single bumper in it. Bonus points if a car sneaks in at the very last second.
card.good_to_know: The bends were built in 1922 to soften a natural 27 percent grade that was too steep for most vehicles. The block is about 180 metres long, one-way downhill and paved with red bricks. Take the Powell-Hyde cable car to the top and you can walk down on the sidewalk or the stairs.

card.hook: Most chocolate factories hide their sign. Ghirardelli's got turned around to face the water, so the sign greets you from the bay side, brick buildings and all.
card.stand_here: Stand in Aquatic Park, across the street from the square on the waterfront side. The square is to the south-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so face south-west and you'll have the sign and the brick buildings in front of you, with the bay behind you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the sign and buildings together. If the square looks small and far away, try 2x or higher (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the sign and the brickwork. Save 0.5x for when you want lots of sky and foreground, because the square will shrink.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the sign on one of the upper lines with the brick buildings below it, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go around sunset if you can, when the bay turns gold and the sign comes on. It's busy most of the time, so wait a moment for gaps in the crowd before you tap the shutter button.
card.selfie_here: Head behind the square, near The Cheese School of San Francisco, where one guide describes a quieter patio with bay views (it's only mentioned in one guide, so treat it as a maybe). Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and put the view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by in Aquatic Park, across from the square, and ask them to frame the sign together with the bay behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay alert around pedestrians and trailing cables while you set up. If you try Hyde Street Pier for a second angle, keep to the pier edge. You don't need to board the historic ships for the photo, and boarding them is ticketed.
card.challenge: Can you get the sign, the red brick and a sailboat all in one frame, with the horizon dead level?
card.good_to_know: Domenico Ghirardelli bought the whole city block in 1893 for his chocolate company. In 1964 it reopened as a restaurant and shopping complex, the first major re-use project of its kind in the United States. Hyde Street Pier gives a second view back across the water, with the historic ships in the foreground.

card.hook: Picture a floating dock so packed with sea lions that they're basically shoving each other for elbow room. They doze, bark and pile up, and you get to watch from just a few steps away.
card.stand_here: Stand on K-Dock, along the sea lion docks at Pier 39. The pier itself is a short way to the north-east, so face the floating docks with the pier's sign and the bay or skyline behind the animals.
card.zoom: Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the sea lions. Switch back to zoom 1x when you want the pier sign and the bay in the shot too.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the nearest sea lion, then slide the picture a bit darker if the bright water or sky is washing out their fur.
card.best_time: Early morning, before about 10am, is your best bet for livelier sea lions and a quieter pier. Numbers are highest from autumn through early spring, and in summer many head off to breed, so the docks can look much emptier.
card.selfie_here: Try the decks on the west side of Pier 39, standing at the pier's edge with the sea lions nearby. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the open bay behind you, but the pier itself won't be in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Stand near the far end of the sea lion viewing platform and ask a passer-by to shoot back toward you, so the floating docks, the Pier 39 sign and the skyline sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep behind the barriers, keep a respectful distance from the sea lions and don't disturb them. The sea lion viewing area may change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Put the sea lions in the lower third with gridlines on, then try to catch a bark with a Live Photo.
card.good_to_know: Pier 39 opened on 4 October 1978. The first sea lions hauled out on its docks in September 1989, and the crowds have followed ever since. As many as 1,700 were reported in Thanksgiving week 2009, while the reported maximum in May 2024 was 1,100 to 1,200.

card.hook: Most people snap Oracle Park from the front door, but the better shot is from across the water. From there the stadium, the bay, the Bay Bridge and the downtown skyline all squeeze into one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in China Basin Park, on the south shore of McCovey Cove, directly across the water from the ballpark. Face the stadium's right-field side, with the cove in front of you and the Bay Bridge and skyline behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the cove, the ballpark and the bridge together. Zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the stadium and the bridge, or drop to 0.5x if it's crowded and you want to keep the water in front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water along the bottom third, keep the horizon level, then tap the stadium and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening is the sweet spot, when the light is softer and the ballpark and bridge are lit up. Match days are busy, so go earlier or on a non-match day if you want a clearer view.
card.selfie_here: Head to the bronze Willie Mays statue at Willie Mays Plaza by the main entrance. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if you want more stadium), keep the ballpark over your shoulder, and aim for golden hour when the stadium lights add some drama. The giant baseball glove in the Fan Lot is another fun spot with the ballpark behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in China Basin Park on the far side of the cove and frame you with the ballpark behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official Oracle Park policy if you're carrying anything bigger than your phone. It's also worth checking whether you need a ticket to reach the glove in the Fan Lot.
card.challenge: Can you get the water on the bottom third, a dead-level horizon and the Bay Bridge peeking out beside the stadium, all in one shot?
card.good_to_know: Oracle Park is the home of the San Francisco Giants and opened on 31 March 2000. It has been called Pacific Bell Park and AT&T Park, and Oracle bought the name in 2019. The bit of bay beyond the right-field wall is unofficially McCovey Cove, named after former Giants player Willie McCovey.

The Willie Mays statue was also listed as a photo spot in several other guides, but only the two sources cited describe the stadium behind it.

card.hook: Picture a Roman ruin that's way too tidy, sitting beside a pond that was built to be a mirror. That's the Palace of Fine Arts, and on a still day the lagoon does exactly what it was designed to do.
card.stand_here: Stand on the opposite bank of the lagoon from the rotunda, in the Marina District. Face west across the water, with the rotunda straight ahead and the colonnades curving off to each side.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the rotunda, colonnades and reflection all in one go. If trees or the water's edge stop you stepping back, try 0.5x. Use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) when you want a tighter shot of the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the horizon and colonnade up with them, then tap the rotunda and slide it a little darker so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Weekday early mornings or late afternoons tend to be quieter. A calm day gives the clearest reflection, and wind can spoil it, so skip Live Photos if the water's rippling.
card.selfie_here: Walk into the curved colonnade, stand a few columns deep and lean on a column. Use the front camera (0.5x if yours has it) and let the repeating pillars frame you with the Palace behind your shoulder. The small stone bridge by the lagoon is a backup spot for a wider backdrop, though it's the weaker pick.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite bank of the lagoon, across from the rotunda, so the whole dome and its reflection sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are listed as banned for events at the Palace theatre (from an unofficial bag-policy site), so check before you bring one. Don't leave anything on display in your car, as break-ins are a worry at the parking areas.
card.challenge: Get the dome and its reflection in one frame, with the water filling the bottom third and the horizon dead level on the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Bernard Maybeck designed the Palace for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition as a make-believe Roman ruin. It's the only structure from that fair still standing on its original site. The first version was wood and plaster, so it was rebuilt in concrete between 1964 and 1974, and the open rotunda is about 49 metres (162 feet) high.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the opposite bank of the lagoon from the rotunda, in the Marina District. Face west across the water, with the rotunda straight ahead and the colonnades curving off to each side.

card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a lower or upper line, then tap the sky and slide it a touch darker so the colours hold.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset gives softer light and fewer harsh reflections. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone on something steady.

card.hook: Coit Tower is the pale, slim thing poking up above the Telegraph Hill rooftops, like it's peeking over a fence to see what you're up to. Because it stands out so well, it's an easy landmark for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand. The tower is 218 m to the south, so face south. Lombard Street is a separate, optional spot well over a kilometre to the west.
card.zoom: From 218 m away, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer. Zoom 1x shows more of your surroundings but makes the tower look small. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want a wide scene with the tower tiny in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, leaving the lower part of the picture for foreground. Tap the tower, then drag the brighter/darker slider a touch darker so the pale concrete keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because the tower stands out best against a bright, clear sky. Check current conditions before you set out.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawn around the base of the tower in Pioneer Park. Use the front camera and tilt it up so the tower rises over your shoulder, with the park's trees around you. For a leafier shot, go midway down the wooden Filbert Street Steps with the tower above the greenery behind you. Be warned, it's a long, steep climb.
card.rules_and_safety: If you head to Lombard Street, keep to the pavement, as it's a busy public street. The tower's observation deck and interior may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Walk up to the main entrance and get a close-up of the concrete phoenix above the door.
card.good_to_know: Coit Tower is 210 feet (64 m) tall and made of unpainted reinforced concrete, which gives it that pale Art Deco look. It was built in 1932-33 with money left by Lillie Hitchcock Coit to beautify the city. It stands in Pioneer Park.

card.hook: Most people snap the Dragon Gate once from the corner and move on. You're going to get two very different photos here: a big one and a close one.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon at the foot of the Dragon Gate, right beside the stone lions, and face the gate. For the full-gate shot later, walk to the corner of Grant Avenue and Bush Street.
card.zoom: Use 1x for the lions and the base of the gate. Then tilt up and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the roof tiles, dragons and the carved characters above you.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lion, then slide the picture a little darker if the bright sky is washing out the green tiles.
card.best_time: Go when it's less busy if you want fewer people around the lions, and check the light when you arrive. The gate is on a public street, so you can visit freely at any time.
card.selfie_here: Step inside one of the two smaller side arches (not the wide central one) so the green-tiled roofline is right behind you. Or pose beside one of the stone lions with the gate filling the background. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it, to fit in more of the gate.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the south side of Bush Street facing north, far enough back to fit all three portals, while you stand by the lions so they frame you.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic runs through this junction, so stay on the pavement and crossings. Wait for a lull before crossing Bush Street, and don't stand in the road to get your shot.
card.challenge: Find both lions: the one with a paw on a pearl or stone, and the one with a paw on a young lion. Get a close-up of each, with the face on a third line of your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The Dragon Gate was built in 1969 and formally dedicated in October 1970. The tiles and the guardian lions were made and donated by Taiwan. The male lion is at the west portal and the female at the east. The four characters above the central portal are a motto attributed to Sun Yat-sen.

card.hook: San Francisco's skyline has one very sharp point, and from Columbus Avenue the whole street seems to run straight at it. It's the Transamerica Pyramid, and it makes any photo look like you planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Columbus Avenue and Kearny Street. Face south-east down Columbus Avenue, and the pyramid sits at the far end of the street.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole street and the tower fit. If your phone has 2x, try it to bring the spire closer. 0.5x shows more street but makes the tower look small.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't turn white and the building keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Wait for the fog to clear, because it makes for a better shot. Morning or late afternoon is good too, when the light on the tower changes.
card.selfie_here: Try the end of the wooden Pier 7 on the Embarcadero, between the Ferry Building and Pier 39. Its Victorian lamps and lanterns frame the pyramid. Use the front camera at 0.5x and try to fit the tower over your shoulder, but check the framing on site, because we can't tell you which way to face. The pier wobbles a bit, so plant your feet.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by, stand near the Columbus and Kearny corner, and ask them to shoot south along Columbus Avenue so the pyramid sits at the end of the street.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed in public areas such as the lobby and Redwood Park at the building's base. The tower's observation deck is closed. One general San Francisco guide says the area is mostly safe in daylight, but advises against walking the quieter blocks late at night with a visible camera bag.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the spire dead centre on the street, and wait for a gap in the traffic. Bonus points if nobody walks through your shot.
card.good_to_know: The Transamerica Pyramid is at 600 Montgomery Street and has 48 storeys, reaching 853 feet (260 m). It was finished in 1972 and was the city's tallest building until 2017. The pyramid shape was chosen to let more light reach the street below. Not everyone liked it at first, but it's now one of the city's symbols.

card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the monument on a centre or side line, and keep the phone level so the column stands up straight.

card.hook: Everyone rushes through the gate to find the famous bridge, but the garden looks pretty good from the road outside too. Red rooftops and soft green trees, with no queue.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the garden and its greenery together. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one pagoda roof or lantern. Use 0.5x only if you can step back, because it can make the garden look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then nudge it a little darker so the greens and red paintwork stay rich.
card.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, and the soft morning light is lovely on the greenery. Check the garden's hours before you go, because some of the best views are inside.

card.hook: Picture a chunky brick fort with a giant steel bridge perched right on top of it, like a hat that's a bit too big. That's Fort Point, and it's a great place to feel tiny in the best way.
card.stand_here: Walk out onto Torpedo Wharf, the pier between Fort Point and Crissy Field, and stand near the rail. The fort is to the west, so face the bridge and keep the fort just off to one side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bridge, the rail and the water in one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arch and the fort's brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the bridge deck up with a horizontal line, then use the pier rail to lead the eye towards the bridge.
card.best_time: Pick a clear spell when fog and low cloud aren't hiding the bridge. Soft light early or late in the day tends to flatter the steel.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Battery East Vista above the fort, where the fort sits below you and the bridge beyond. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little high and let the bridge sit over your shoulder. Down on the waterside outside the fort works too, but there the bridge is the star and the fort plays second fiddle.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Battery East Vista and ask a passer-by to take your photo so Fort Point shows beneath you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's often very windy here, so hold your phone with both hands and keep a firm grip. The fort's interior and roof are open only on certain days, so check the National Park Service site before you go.
card.challenge: Snap the pier rail leading straight to the bridge, then take a second shot with a friend 'holding up' the arch.
card.good_to_know: The US Army built the fort you see today just before the Civil War, with walls seven feet thick. Workers cut the 90-foot cliff down to 15 feet above sea level to keep its guns close to the water. When the bridge was planned in the 1930s, engineer Joseph Strauss changed his design so the fort could stay, and it became a National Historic Site in 1970.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk out onto Torpedo Wharf, the pier between Fort Point and Crissy Field, and stand near the rail. The fort is to the west, so face the bridge and keep the fort just off to one side.

card.hook: Most people shoot Twin Peaks from the top, which is a bit like photographing a cake while standing on it. Climb the rocky summit of Corona Heights Park instead and you see both hills on the skyline with the whole city spread out below.
card.stand_here: Stand on the rocky summit of Corona Heights Park and turn to face the peaks on the skyline, with the city below you. It's quieter than the top of Twin Peaks, and you get to see the hills as a whole.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a wide shot with the city below. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the peaks closer. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the hills look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the peaks on the upper line, fill the bottom with rooftops and streets, and tap the peaks, then slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because fog often hides the view, especially in the morning. Earlier in the day the sun is behind you. Late on it's in front of you, and the peaks look flatter against the glare.
card.selfie_here: Try the north peak overlook at the top of Twin Peaks. Use the front camera, hold it a little higher, and get the city over your shoulder. Christmas Tree Point near the summit parking is another good spot for a view-behind-you selfie.
card.ask_someone: At the low wall at the foot of Twin Peaks, where a wedding couple was once photographed sitting, you can sit on the wall and ask a passer-by to take your photo from a few steps back.
card.rules_and_safety: Lock valuables out of sight and don't leave bags in a parked car, because car break-ins are the main problem at the Twin Peaks parking area. It can get windy, so hold your phone firmly.
card.challenge: Get both peaks, a slice of rocky summit and a rooftop in one shot, then see if a friend can spot where you were standing.
card.good_to_know: Twin Peaks are about 925 feet (282 m) high, making them the second and third highest natural points in San Francisco. Only Mount Davidson is higher, by a few feet. The North and South summits are roughly 200 m apart. The west-facing slopes often catch fog and strong wind, so the view can change quickly.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the rocky summit of Corona Heights Park and turn to face the peaks on the skyline, with the city below you. It's quieter than the top of Twin Peaks, and you get to see the hills as a whole.

card.hook: Standing right at Grace Cathedral's front door gives you a sore neck and a photo of mostly steps. Cross the street into the park and the whole spire fits, with trees dressing up the edges.
card.stand_here: Stand in Huntington Park, on the east side of the park, and face west across Taylor Street toward the cathedral's front. You'll see the Gothic facade and spire with the park's trees around the edges.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the facade and spire in one shot. Use 0.5x only if trees or fences force you to stand close, and keep the building upright so the edges don't lean. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the rose window and the top of the spire.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to line the spire up with a vertical line, and if the sky is bright, tap the stonework instead of the sky so the facade doesn't turn dark.
card.best_time: Daylight is best for the full view from the park, when the whole facade is clearly lit. At dusk you can try the rose window from Taylor Street, but only if its lighting is switched on, so have the daylight shot banked first. The steps at the western edge of the park are noted as best around the 6 p.m. bell-ringing hour.
card.selfie_here: Try the top of the steps at the western edge of Huntington Park, a raised spot with the cathedral's front in view. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and turn so the spire sits over your shoulder. Check the cathedral actually fits behind you before you snap.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the sidewalk across Taylor Street, mid-block, where photographers set up just before dark, and stand in front of the cathedral so the facade fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is public and there's no fee for the view. If you want to go inside the cathedral, check the official website before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots in one visit: a wide one with the trees, a tight one of the spire, and one of the rose window. Then pick your favourite and brag about it.
card.good_to_know: Grace Cathedral is a Gothic-style church with a tall spire and a rose window above the front door. California Street gives a different view, with the front and rose window at an angle and the cable car line in the foreground. It adds a bit of San Francisco character to your shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Huntington Park, on the east side of the park, and face west across Taylor Street toward the cathedral's front. You'll see the Gothic facade and spire with the park's trees around the edges.

card.hook: You've probably seen these seven pastel houses before, even if you've never been to San Francisco: they open Full House. The fun part is finding the spot where the downtown towers pop up right behind them.
card.stand_here: Stand in Alamo Square Park, on the upper grassy slope on the west side of Steiner Street, climbing toward the crest. Face the row of houses across the street and shuffle a few steps left or right until the towers clear the rooftops.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole row with the skyline behind it. If the towers look tiny, try zoom 2x, and save zoom 0.5x for close-ups when you're down by the houses. Keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the rooflines straight, then tap the houses and drag a little darker so the sky keeps its detail and the colours look rich.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset is lovely, with warm light on the fronts of the houses. Early morning is usually quieter. Fog often hides the skyline, especially in summer, so grab a plain-houses shot as your backup.
card.selfie_here: Try the grassy upper slope inside Alamo Square Park, on the grass uphill from Steiner Street, where you get a clear line to the row. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, hold your phone a bit high, and try to fit the houses over your shoulder. Check the screen before you shoot, as you may need to turn a little to get them in.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand uphill on the sloped lawn at the northeast corner of the park, about the second row of benches, while you stand on the Steiner Street pavement in front of the houses. Tell them to climb high enough that other people don't block the row.
card.rules_and_safety: The houses are private homes, so photograph them only from the street and the park, and keep clear of the doorways.
card.challenge: Find the exact spot where all seven houses sit under the towers with no tree in the way, then take one shot with the skyline and one with just the colours.
card.good_to_know: Developer Matthew Kavanaugh built these Victorian houses at 710-720 Steiner Street between 1892 and 1896. The bright paint is much newer: San Francisco's colourful repaint movement began in the 1960s, and the 'painted ladies' name took off after a 1978 book. The row has appeared in an estimated 70 films, TV programmes and adverts, which is why it feels so familiar.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Alamo Square Park, on the upper grassy slope on the west side of Steiner Street, climbing toward the crest. Face the row of houses across the street and shuffle a few steps left or right until the towers clear the rooftops.

card.hook: Picture a pale white greenhouse on a gentle rise, with a glass dome and curved wings, looking like a stage set for a postcard. That's the Conservatory of Flowers, and it really does look this good in person.
card.stand_here: Stand in Conservatory Valley, on the lawn and formal flower beds right in front of the building. Face north and the conservatory is straight ahead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full-building postcard shot. Switch to zoom 0.5x if the flower beds and fountain matter as much as the building. Try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to home in on the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome on the centre line so both wings balance, then tap the white facade and slide it a touch darker so the glass and paintwork don't wash out.
card.best_time: Right before sunset is the recommended time for outdoor photos here. The very pale building stands out nicely against the green lawn and trees.
card.selfie_here: Head to the lawn below the building, near the 'Love blocks' sculptures, and use the front camera at 0.5x with the hilltop conservatory rising behind you. From late June to late October you can also try the dahlia beds in the roundabout on the building's right-hand side for a colourful foreground.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on John F Kennedy Drive, the road running past the building, to take a wider shot of you with the building and the park's trees behind.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go inside, take care with your phone in the Potted Plants room. Plants hang high there and sometimes drip water. Entry to the building may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots from three spots a few steps apart, then see which one gets the flower beds sitting prettiest in front of the dome.
card.good_to_know: The central dome rises nearly 60 feet (18 m), and the curved glass wings stretch the building to about 240 feet (73 m). Building work finished in 1879, which makes it the oldest building in Golden Gate Park. The front view also works when the building is closed.

card.hook: Picture a 245-foot clock tower parked at the very end of Market Street, like the full stop on a very long sentence. For decades a freeway hid it, so it's a treat that you can just walk up and look at it now.
card.stand_here: Stand at the foot of Market Street on The Embarcadero and face the clock tower. This gets you a close view of the tower and the end of the street; the classic squeezed-together shot is taken from much further west up Market Street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the building and the end of the street in the frame. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower, and hold the phone with both hands.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide darker just a little so the sky and clock faces keep their detail, and turn on gridlines to keep the tower standing up straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or a weekday is easiest, with fewer people in your way. Skip Saturday mornings, when the farmers market fills the front, and the hours around Giants games.
card.selfie_here: Head to Harry Bridges Plaza, out front of the main entrance, and pose with the clock tower behind you. The Vaillancourt Fountain in front of the building is another easy spot. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up so the tower peeks over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Walk out on the pier on the left side of the building as you face it and ask someone to photograph you with the Ferry Building behind you. One guide says the view from there is great, especially at night.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask permission before taking lots of photos inside the individual shops in the Ferry Building. The terminals, food hall and offices may have their own hours and rules, so check the official site.
card.challenge: Step up close to the long row of arches along the front, go wide at 0.5x, and see how many arches you can squeeze into one shot.
card.good_to_know: The architect A. Page Brown designed the Ferry Building in the Beaux-Arts style, and it opened in 1898. The tower has four clock dials, each 22 feet (6.7 m) across. It came through both the 1906 and 1989 earthquakes with little damage, and it still has working ferry terminals and a food hall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the foot of Market Street on The Embarcadero and face the clock tower. This gets you a close view of the tower and the end of the street; the classic squeezed-together shot is taken from much further west up Market Street.
